entry.title: Pigeons (Columba livia) as Trainable Observers of Pathology and Radiology Breast Cancer Images

link.title: Pigeons (Columba livia) as Trainable Observers of Pathology and Radiology Breast Cancer Images

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 17

Today’s paper is one of those “could be cool” kinds of experiment. Skinner did get an Ig Nobel for pigeon missiles, after all, so why can’t pigeon histopathologists work just as well? And yup, they do. The experiment design was eerily similar to basic machine learning, complete with dataset augmentation via rotating and flipping the images. Looking at those tissue images myself, I really cannot tell which ones are benign, and which are malignant, but evidently, pigeons, who spent several weeks practicing every day, could do it quite easily. Mammograms proved much harder to distinguish, but human experts kinda struggle with them too. Overall, an impressive performance from the avian “doctors”

entry.title: Fitting A Person Into An NMR Spectrometer

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 16

Today’s paper is from a venerable publication called The Journal of Immaterial Science that since 2021 has been getting out chuckles and snorts immune to the reproducibility crisis. Having worked several years in an NMR lab, I find this particular paper especially hilarious. The fact that the 900 MHz UltraWide-Bore NMR spectrometer actually exists and actually has been used for imaging live rodents is just the icing on the cake XD

entry.title: Magneto-Optical Detection of the Spin Hall Effect in Pt and W Thin Films

link.title: Magneto-Optical Detection of the Spin Hall Effect in Pt and W Thin Films

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 15

Today’s paper is a continuation of my exploration of ways of measuring spin Hall effect. This time, the technique uses magneto-optic Kerr effect: spin Hall effect leads to spin accumulation on the surface of the wire, and thus, if you light the wire up with a laser, the polarization of reflected light rotates. The spatial distribution of accumulated spins depends on sample thickness. So if you measure Kerr rotation for a bunch of samples of various thicknesses, you can extract the spin Hall angle. The coolest part of this technique is that it allows to measure the SHE more or less directly, unlike pretty much every single other method I’ve found so far, which all require the SHE material to interact somehow with a ferromagnet.

entry.title: High-throughput techniques for measuring the spin Hall effect

link.title: High-throughput techniques for measuring the spin Hall effect

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 14

Today’s paper is again for work, as will probably be several following ones. I’m trying to figure out methods for measuring SHE (awful abbreviation, makes it annoying to search), and this paper was a great start for that.

The three methods covered here are for sure not the only ones, but afaict from reading other papers all three are reasonably commonly used nowadays. They are: terahertz emission spectroscopy (TSE), vector-network analyzer ferromagnetic resonance (VNA FMR) and harmonic Hall response (HHR). TSE: smack sample with femtosecond laser, catch the induced terahertz emission, intensity gives spin Hall angle. VNA FMR: lay sample on waveguide with gigahertz current, measure waveguide’s transmission as function of external magnetic field, do some maths jiggery-pokery and get spin Hall angle. HHR: lithography a cross in your sample, drive an AC current through one arm, measure voltage across the other as function of external magnetic field angle.

I’m kinda hoping I’ll have a chance to try TSE with my own hands, ‘cuz it sounds like pure sci-fi magic, but that one feels like the least generally accessible method. More likely I’ll be doing more “conventional” measurements with Hall crosses and a bunch of lithography, ion beams, and pretty electron microscope photos.

entry.title: Observation of the magnetic spin Hall effect in a ferromagnet

link.title: Observation of the magnetic spin Hall effect in a ferromagnet

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 13

Today’s paper is for work, rather than purely for fun. I still don’t feel I understand everything the authors did, and why they did that, but here’s what I got. They made a device for producing and measuring spin Hall effect in a choice material. The material in question – a stack of thin films of Co and Pt, which really wants to be magnetised perpendicularly to the stack. (Note to self: read up on the methods of fabrication of such devices.) Then, if an electric current \(I_{\text{bias}}\) is passed along the stack (dubbed in this case the injector), for reasons that are still unclear to me, electrons with opposite directions of spin get deflected in the opposite directions, perpendicular to the current and the magnetisation of the injector. They flow through a magnetically neutral wire (copper in this case) and get measured at a magnetised detector (here made out of permalloy). Apparently, (once again, for reasons unclear to me as of yet), the magnetisation of the injector forces a very different behaviour on spins with polarisation transverse to the bias current (conventional SHE, even under time reversal) and parallel to it (magnetic SHE, odd under time reversal). And if you exchange the injector and detector, you can use a spin current to induce an electric current. The “nonlocal resistance” (measured voltage on the detector over the bias current) is the same for the inverse effect, though. Yada, yada, they do a bunch of measurements on their device and confirm the above, as is expected from theory.

Tbh, reading this was unnecessarily annoying for two reasons. Firstly, it felt like reading a novel from page 300: there’s very clearly a lot of stuff the reader is expected to be familiar with, like, say, the conventional spin Hall effect, or the “lateral spin valve” architecture of their device. I am unfamiliar with a lot of that stuff, so it wasn’t a very good paper to get into the topic. Secondly (maybe somewhat related to the first point), abbreviations are EVIL. When a single figure has six of them, I’d say this is too many abbreviations. Way too many.

entry.title: Ancient Egyptian Cereal Processing: Beyond the Artistic Record

link.title: Ancient Egyptian Cereal Processing: Beyond the Artistic Record

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 12

Why archaeology today? Welllll, I was ordering a bunch of cereals, and wondered which ones were used in ancient Egypt (the answer is mostly emmer and barley), as one does, and…

Anyway, today’s paper is a bit of a rant, just the way I like them. This paper is sorta the author yelling at her colleagues (in a very civil manner as behooves a scientific paper): “Let’s maybe stop making chaff up and test our hypotheses with our hands for once?” (not a quote). It’s an opposition to the view of “everything we need to know is drawn on the walls”. I feel like it’s a very wise idea: regardless of whether the experimental (and etnographic, and biological, and archaeological) evidence leads one to an entirely accurate reconstruction of the past or not, it’s still going to be a better reconstruction than one that only uses a single source of information.

entry.title: Soil health assessment using buried cotton underpants with the help of 1000 citizen scientists

link.title: Soil health assessment using buried cotton underpants with the help of 1000 citizen scientists

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 11

Today’s paper speaks for itself. While it was as much an awareness campaign as a scientific study, it was quite successful at both. Underpants decomposition does indeed provide a reasonable proxy for soil microbial activity (at least comparable with other existing heuristics), and it is just funny enough for a bunch of people to participate. And the quote “Underwear was mainly buried in areas where population density is higher and rarely in the mountains” is just delightful out of context.

entry.title: Reconstructing food plant terms and associated terminologies in Proto Oceanic

link.title: Reconstructing food plant terms and associated terminologies in Proto Oceanic

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 10

Today’s paper is the first installment of linguistics here. I haven’t read ling papers for months, turns out I missed them :-) This one is mostly a giant sequence of cognate lists together with a reconstruction of the POc root, but there were a few curious comments that make it worth reading. The funniest one is the coconut issue: a lot of Oceanic langs have a bunch (7-9) of distinct words designating various growth stages of a coconut (like, green and ready to drink vs dry and ready to fall, etc). That is not surprising by itself. However, the words different languages use for these different coconuts are not cognates. The semantic categories are very stable across the board, but it seems like everyone made their own terms for them.

Of course, I read the paper with Te Aka Māori dictionary trying to figure out which reflexes survived. One funny find was that renga (yellow) comes from PEOc *reŋ(ʷ)a that meant “turmeric”. It makes sense, but still funny. Another find that I cannot find evidence for, but strongly suspect nonetheless is that uri (offspring, descendant, kin) comes from POc *(s,j)uli(q) – plant sucker, cutting, shoot. While that cognate set does not have words meaning “relative” and all of them are bananas, taro, or their parts, the fact that hua can also mean descendant makes the plant metaphor more plausible to my eyes. Also, pū (bunch, tuft, bundle) that according to wiktionary comes from POc *puqu (origin, base of a tree) could be related to POc *puŋu – meaning “bunch”.

Sheesh, I think I miss te reo… Maybe it’s time to try learning it again. Maybe next attempt is gonna be more fruitful than all previous ones?

entry.title: A decagon wave around Saturn’s south pole

link.title: A decagon wave around Saturn’s south pole

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 9

I’m not gonna write about seven papers today, for each day I missed, but I already wrote a post about this one before my laptop went unresponsive, I like it and I’d like to keep a link to it.

Saturn’s north pole hexagon has been known for a while, but nothing similar has ever been seen on the south pole. Well, now, there’s a decagon. Seemingly it only appeared around four years ago. A giant rotating decagon. Ain’t it the coolest? The paper’s authors took all observations of Saturn they could find and figured out, what the conditions around it are (it sits on a jet, next to a strong anticyclone), how it moves (mostly at a constant angular velocity but with a slight periodic wobble). Then they threw the data into a bunch of shallow water simulations, attempting to reproduce the decagon. They did get some stable 10 sided waves, but not exactly with the same location and speed as the real thing. But still cool they got anything at all. Maybe at some point someone will bother with a multilayered model, and get out more accurate results.

entry.title: The electromotive force produced by the acceleration of metals

link.title: The electromotive force produced by the acceleration of metals

entry.content:
A paper a day: day 8

I missed an entire week, but I have a good excuse: my laptop developed a rapidly progressing dementia just as I was writing a post, and I had literally no way to post anything for a while. I’m back, and hopefully won’t have such technical issues again any time soon.

Today’s paper I actually read several days ago, while preparing for the PhD program entrance exams. Very cool experiment, wonder why it isn’t taught in high school physics. Imagine, you’re in a time before it was known for certain electrons are what carries charge in metals. Electron itself is known, but not whether the charge carrier is that or something else. How do you test whether it is electrons? Mandelstam & Papalexi (whose paper I could not find, afaict their experiment was never written up as a proper paper), and then Tolman & Stewart (making the experiment quantitative) decided to use the fact that electrons have a known mass. They quickly rotated a copper coil, and then abrubptly stopped it. But electrons, due to intertia, continued moving. Mandelstam & Papalexi had a phone attached to their coil, and they heard a sound. Tolman & Stewart had a ballistic galvanometer, so they actually measured the charge that flowed through the coil, and thus measured the charge carrier’s mass (mass to charge ratio, actually, but never mind). It turned out to be pretty dang close to the mass of an electron in a vacuum. Really surprised it actually worked. They had to get rid of the Earth’s magnetic field for that, for crying out loud… But it WORKED!
